summary: The TRILL base protocol (RFC 6325) leaves minimal hooks for safely extending its header. This document specifies an initial extension that provides additional flag bits and defines some of those bits. It updates RFC 6325.

eli5.summary: The label on a package had no room for more notes. This adds extra check boxes and uses some of them.

questions: what is the trill header extension
what are trill critical summary bits
what is the trill channel alert flag
how big can a trill header extension be
subtitle: How TRILL headers carry optional extra flags safely, and the first two flags defined for it.

tldr.problem: The TRILL base protocol has only minimal hooks for extending its header, so there was no defined structure for extensions and no way to be sure that switches that do not understand an extension handle it safely.
tldr.mechanism: An initial 32-bit word of extended flags follows the fixed TRILL header, with three critical summary bits that tell each switch quickly whether it must drop the frame, plus hop-by-hop, ingress-to-egress and reserved flag groups.
tldr.outcome: Two flags are defined, the Critical and Non-critical Channel Alert flags used by RBridge Channel messages. RFC 7780 later updated this document.

today: RFC 7179 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014 and has been updated by RFC 7780. It updates RFC 6325 and is not marked as obsoleted.

sections.title: Extending the TRILL Header
sections.content:
The base TRILL protocol in RFC 6325 includes a feature for extending the TRILL header, called options in its Section 3.8, with minimal hooks to support extensions safely. Apart from the first two bits, it does not specify what an extension looks like or define any particular one.

This document stays consistent with RFC 6325 and adds detail. It specifies an initial extension word of flag bits and defines some of those bits. It updates RFC 6325. Further extensions, including TLV-encoded options, may be specified in later documents.
sections.eli5: The original label had a spot for extras but no rules. This RFC adds the rules and the first extra boxes.

sections.title: Critical and Non-critical Extensions
sections.content:
The 5-bit Op-Length field gives the length of the header extensions in units of 4 octets, which allows up to 124 octets of extension. If it is zero there are no extensions. Otherwise the extension area follows the Ingress RBridge Nickname field, and its first 32-bit word holds the extended flags.

Flags are grouped three ways: hop-by-hop flags that may affect any RBridge on the path, ingress-to-egress flags that only need to affect RBridges that decapsulate, and reserved flags for a class of RBridges to be specified later, such as border RBridges in a multi-level IS-IS campus. Each group has critical and non-critical flags.

  • An RBridge that gets a critical hop-by-hop extension it does not implement MUST discard the frame.
  • An egress RBridge that gets an unimplemented critical ingress-to-egress extension MUST drop a unicast frame (M=0). For a multi-destination frame (M=1) it MUST NOT egress the frame, but it still forwards it on the distribution tree.
  • Non-critical extensions can be safely ignored.

Any flag that changes the structure or interpretation of later parts of the frame, so that ignoring it could break service or violate security policy, MUST be critical. If it affects fields that transit RBridges examine, it MUST be a hop-by-hop critical flag.
sections.eli5: Some notes say 'ignore me if you cannot read me' and others say 'if you cannot read this, throw the whole package away.' The second kind is called critical.

sections.title: The Extended Header Flags Word
sections.content:
When extensions are present, the first 32 bits form the extended header flags word. Any RBridge adding an extensions area MUST start with those bits all zero unless a flag permits otherwise, and transit RBridges transparently copy the word apart from permitted modifications.

The first three bits are the critical summary bits. CHbHS says critical hop-by-hop extensions are present, CItES says critical ingress-to-egress extensions are present, and CRSVS says critical reserved extensions are present. The rest of the word is split into flag groups: bits 3-7 critical hop-by-hop, 8-13 non-critical hop-by-hop, 14-16 critical reserved, 17-20 non-critical reserved, 21-26 critical ingress-to-egress and 27-31 non-critical ingress-to-egress.

The summary bits make processing cheap. An RBridge that supports no critical extensions need only check whether Op-Length is non-zero and, if so, look at the top one, two or three bits. A transit RBridge that does not support all critical hop-by-hop extensions MUST drop a frame with CHbHS set. If both CHbHS and CItES are zero, the frame is safe for an egress RBridge to process whatever it supports.
sections.eli5: The first three boxes are like red warning stickers on the outside of the package. A switch only has to look at those stickers, not read everything inside.

sections.title: What RBridges Must Do
sections.content:
All RBridges MUST check whether any critical flags apply to their processing. If an RBridge does not implement all the critical flags in a frame, it treats the frame as having an unimplemented critical extension. A transit or egress RBridge may assume the critical summary bits are correct.

A transit RBridge MAY set or clear hop-by-hop flags as specified for them. If it adds or removes the flags word it MUST adjust Op-Length. If it adds the word or changes critical flags it MUST set the summary bits correctly. It MUST NOT remove the flags word unless it is all zero, and MUST NOT set or clear ingress-to-egress or reserved flags except where permitted.

To avoid surprises, RBridges advertise the extended header flags they support in IS-IS PDUs (RFC 7176), and an RBridge SHOULD NOT set a critical flag unless it has determined that the relevant next hop or egress RBridges support it. Conflicting extensions SHOULD NOT be defined.

Header extensions may push frames onto a slower processing path, and limited slow path throughput could cause some of those frames to be discarded.
sections.eli5: Switches must obey the stickers, keep them right if they change them, and only add a critical sticker when the next switch can understand it.

sections.title: The Channel Alert Flags
sections.content:
The only two flags defined here are the Critical Channel Alert flag (bit 7) and the Non-critical Channel Alert flag (bit 8). Both mark a frame as an RBridge Channel message (RFC 7178) that asks for processing at each hop.

If the Critical flag is set and an RBridge does not implement the RBridge Channel feature or the channel protocol, or the frame does not look like a channel message, the frame is discarded. That allows a message such as one needing strict source routing to be dropped rather than stray from its path. The Non-critical flag suits something like a record route function, where skipping RBridges that do not support it is acceptable.
sections.eli5: The channel alert stickers say 'look at this note on the way.' The critical one means 'drop it if you cannot.' The other means 'skip it if you cannot.'

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA created a TRILL Extended Header Flags subregistry populated from the table of flag assignments, and new flags are allocated by IETF Review. It also assigned bits in the TRILL-VER and PORT-TRILL-VER sub-TLV capability flag registries from RFC 7176: bits 3-13 of PORT-TRILL-VER indicate support for hop-by-hop flags 3-13, and bits 14-31 of TRILL-VER indicate support for flags 14-31.

For security, the critical summary bits must be set properly. If set when no matching critical extension exists, frames may be dropped needlessly. If not set when one exists, frames may be mishandled or corrupted and security policy violated. If a Channel Alert flag shows up in a frame that is not a channel message, it MAY be cleared and should only delay processing at worst. If it is wrongly omitted, desired per-hop processing may not happen.
sections.eli5: If the warning stickers are wrong, good packages get thrown away or bad ones get through, so switches must get them right.
